nameStory: Red osier dogwood gets its name from those striking red stems that catch your eye from across a wetland, especially in winter when everything else looks drab. The word 'osier' refers to flexible twigs used in basket weaving, and this shrub's pliable red branches were traditionally woven into baskets by Native Americans. It's also called redtwig dogwood, red willow, and red brush – all names that celebrate those gorgeous crimson stems!
description: Red osier dogwood is a spreading shrub that grows 3-10 feet tall, forming dense colonies through underground runners. Its most striking feature is the bright red to reddish-purple bark on young stems, which creates stunning winter displays in wetlands across New England. In summer, it produces clusters of small white flowers followed by white berries, but those colorful stems steal the show year-round. This native shrub is a wetland champion, thriving where many other plants struggle.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are bright red to deep reddish-purple, smooth to the touch and almost glossy – they practically glow against snow or brown marsh grass. Older stems fade to grayish-brown, so look for the newest growth for the best red color.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves are oval-shaped with prominent curved veins that follow the leaf's outline from base to tip. The leaves feel smooth and somewhat thick, turning reddish or purplish in fall before dropping.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers cluster together in flat-topped groups about 2-4 inches across in late spring to early summer. Each tiny flower has four petals and gives off a subtle, pleasant fragrance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: White berries about the size of peppercorns appear in late summer, often with a slight bluish tint. They feel firm when fresh and are an important food source for birds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through underground runners, creating thickets of upright stems. Individual stems grow straight up from the ground, rarely branching much until near the top.

habitat: Red osier dogwood loves wet feet, thriving in marshes, swamps, stream banks, and pond edges throughout New England. You'll find it in areas that flood seasonally or stay consistently moist, often growing alongside willows, elderberry, and cattails. It tolerates both full sun and partial shade, making it common in wetland edges where forests meet open water.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green and fresh, while the red stems begin their most vibrant display of the year. Small white flower clusters appear in late spring, creating a lovely contrast against the colorful bark.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are fully green and lush, somewhat masking the red stems. White berries develop through late summer, and the plant focuses on growing new red shoots.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn beautiful shades of red, orange, or purple before dropping, while berries ripen to bright white. The red stems become more visible as foliage thins.
seasonality.winter: This is red osier's moment to shine – the leafless red stems create stunning displays against snow and brown vegetation, making it one of the most recognizable winter plants in New England wetlands.

funFact: Red osier dogwood stems get redder in cold weather – the plant actually produces more red pigments as temperatures drop, which is why northern plants and those in exposed locations have the most spectacular winter color!
confusionNotes: The bright red stems make this pretty unmistakable, but silky dogwood also grows in wet areas and has similar white flower clusters. The key difference: silky dogwood has brown stems and fuzzy leaf undersides, while red osier has those signature red stems and smooth leaves. Memory trick: 'Red osier, red stems' – it's right in the name!
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the name 'dogwood' with the famous flowering dogwood tree, red osier dogwood is quite different – it's a shrub that thrives in wet areas while flowering dogwood is a tree preferring well-drained woodland soils. All dogwoods share the characteristic opposite leaves with curved parallel veins, but their habitats and growth forms vary dramatically.
compareHints: Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark. Silky dogwood also likes moisture but has brown stems and fuzzy leaves, while gray dogwood prefers drier sites and has grayish bark. The tree dogwoods like flowering dogwood grow much taller and prefer well-drained forest soils rather than wet areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
